{"id": "74:26/q03", "question": "What does سقر denote?", "turns_on": "Whether Saqar names Hell as a whole, a level or gate within it, a specified part, or an allegorical name for afterlife suffering; reports disagree over its numbered location.", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q03/p1", "position": "Saqar is a name for Hell or its Fire.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ compares the proper name Laẓā. Al-Zajjāj, al-Māwardī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Nasafī, al-Bursawī citing al-Ṣiḥāḥ, and the Study Quran's cited authorities use it as a name of Hell or the Fire. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the majority of commentators use it synonymously with Jahannam, although it can name a place within Hell. Ibn al-Jawzī refers readers to 54:48. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows this alongside a level; the Turkish commentary cites al-Shawkānī for a name of the fire that also denotes a section with severe punishment."}, {"id": "74:26/q03/p2", "position": "Saqar is an unspecified level or section of Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports this alongside gate and name interpretations. Al-Ṭabrisī reports a level as an alternative to Hell and its gate. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows a named place in Hell; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows one of its levels. The Turkish commentary reports al-Shawkānī's description of a section with severe punishment; al-Biqāʿī describes a fiery level whose heat melts the brain. Al-Ṭabarī describes Saqar as a part of Hell named Saqar."}, {"id": "74:26/q03/p3", "position": "Saqar is the sixth level or depth of Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bursawī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr transmit this from Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports the sixth level; Ibn ʿĀshūr notes that Ibn ʿAṭiyya confines his explanation to the sixth depth."}, {"id": "74:26/q03/p4", "position": "Saqar is an unspecified gate of Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī lists a gate among reported explanations; al-Ṭabrisī reports it as an alternative, and the Study Quran cites al-Ṭabarī for it. Al-Ṭabarī also describes Saqar as a gate of Hell."}, {"id": "74:26/q03/p5", "position": "Saqar is Hell's fifth gate.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies the fifth gate."}, {"id": "74:26/q03/p6", "position": "Saqar is the lowest part of Hell, containing the tree of Zaqqūm.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī transmits this from Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Durr al-Manthūr; it differs in detail from the sixth-level reports also attributed to him."}, {"id": "74:26/q03/p7", "position": "Saqar is one of seven metaphorical names for self-incurred suffering in the afterlife.", "reasons": "Asad calls this its earliest Qurʾānic occurrence and attributes that suffering to sin and deliberate blindness to spiritual truth, mentioning 15:33; he reads descriptions here and from 74:28 onward allegorically."}]}
{"id": "74:26/q04", "question": "What is the derivation and lexical force of سقر?", "turns_on": "Whether the name can be derived from Arabic scorching language or is underived or borrowed.", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q04/p1", "position": "It is Arabic-derived from the sun's scorching, melting, or burning heat.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās cites the sun's scorching and al-sāqūr, heated iron used to cauterize a donkey. Al-Māwardī and al-Jishumī add its painful effect on the brain, with al-Jishumī saying the name conveys the Fire's intense pain; he relates the word for a falcon, saqr or sakr, to the severity of its attack. Al-Qurṭubī mentions scorching and burning skin. Al-Bursawī transmits the link with the sun from Ibn ʿAbbās. Elmalılı prefers the Arabic scorching derivation to a foreign origin. The Study Quran reports the expression saqarathu al-shams."}, {"id": "74:26/q04/p2", "position": "It is an Arabicized loanword of unidentified original form and language.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports al-Jawālīqī's view as cited in al-Itqān; Elmalılı mentions a non-Arabic explanation but favors derivation from the sun's heat. Al-Itqān also reports al-Jawālīqī's view that Saqar is foreign."}, {"id": "74:26/q04/p3", "position": "The name has no derivation.", "reasons": "The Study Quran reports this from some commentators without an etymological argument."}]}
{"id": "74:26/q05", "question": "Why is سقر not declined?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q05/p1", "position": "It is a feminine proper name, so it is diptote.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ calls it a proper name like Laẓā; al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Jishumī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr cite proper naming and feminine gender. Al-Naḥḥās prefers this over foreignness, arguing that a three-letter foreign name with a moving middle would normally decline. Ibn ʿĀshūr says feminine pronouns in 74:27 and 74:30 support the gender, whether Saqar names Hell itself or a place within it. Al-Ṭabarī explains its indeclinability by saying that Saqar is one of Hell's names."}]}
{"id": "74:26/q08", "question": "How do the surrounding verses heighten or recall Saqar's threat?", "turns_on": "The notes address different surrounding clauses, one describing Saqar's dread and another possibly referring back to it.", "positions": [{"id": "74:26/q08/p1", "position": "The wording and following question magnify Saqar's dread.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī says the wording magnifies its dread. Ibn ʿĀshūr parses 'What will make you know what Saqar is?' as a circumstantial clause modifying Saqar and says no informant could make its reality known to the Prophet, magnifying its dreadful state. Al-Ṭabarī says the following question asks Muhammad what Saqar is."}, {"id": "74:26/q08/p2", "position": "A later feminine pronoun may refer back to Saqar as a reminder through its threat and horrors.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports this as another possibility, with an omitted noun such as Saqar's mention or description understood."}]}
{"id": "74:31/q07", "question": "What incident prompted the answer that the guards are angels?", "turns_on": "Which reported taunt and speaker elicited the verse.", "positions": [{"id": "74:31/q07/p1", "position": "Abū Jahl mocked the nineteen and challenged Quraysh to overpower the guards; a strongman offered to take seventeen while others took two.", "reasons": "Accounts vary the strongman's name among Abū al-Ashadd, Abū al-Ashaddayn, Abū al-Asad and al-Ḥārith ibn Kalda; some report a ten-to-one challenge, a cowhide feat, or a boast of pushing ten right and nine left. Ibn Kathīr discusses divergent wrestler identifications; Ibn Isḥāq reports later avoidance of public recitation. Al-Suyuti transmits Ibn Ishaq's report that Abu Jahl asked whether a hundred Quraysh could not overcome one guard, with a similar report from Qatada; he also transmits al-Suddi's account that Abu al-Ashadd boasted he could fend off ten guards with his right shoulder and nine with his left."}, {"id": "74:31/q07/p2", "position": "The verse answered an unnamed boast that even the least strong could enter Hell and then reach Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī transmits this alternative preceding boast."}]}
{"id": "74:43/q14", "question": "How do the four confessed faults account for the sinners' persistence in Saqar?", "turns_on": "Whether every person committed all four faults or different people committed different faults.", "positions": [{"id": "74:43/q14/p1", "position": "All four faults together brought each person to the Fire and kept them in Saqar.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī allows that the four vices jointly brought each person to the Fire; their persistence in Saqar resulted from these faults."}, {"id": "74:43/q14/p2", "position": "Different people entered the Fire for different faults among the four, and persisted in Saqar because of them.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī also allows that the faults were distributed across different people; their persistence in Saqar resulted from these faults."}]}
{"id": "75:33/q05", "question": "What does يَتَمَطَّىٰ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the bodily extension is an affected walking gait or a lazy stretch; both can express arrogance.", "positions": [{"id": "75:33/q05/p1", "position": "He struts or swaggers proudly, with an affected gait.", "reasons": "Muqatil associates such walking with Banu al-Mughira; Zayd ibn Aslam and later transmitters with Banu Makhzum. Ibn Abbas calls it conceit or proud strutting. Al-Tabari, al-Farra, al-Zajjaj and others describe twisting or swaying the back; al-Kashshaf, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur note lengthened steps. Ibn Kathir adds gloating, insolence, laziness and lack of purpose. Bursevi says he boasts of denial; Biqai says he should have shown shame and humility. Al-Qurtubi explains the gait as stretching and twisting the back; al-muṭayṭāʾ is also described as swinging or extending the arms."}, {"id": "75:33/q05/p2", "position": "He stretches himself lazily or heavily, a gesture of disregard and arrogance.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi says the word can describe stretching on rising from sleep. Al-Jishumi specifies stretching the belly from laziness. Al-Qurtubi stresses disregard; al-Majma' as quoted by Tabataba'i calls it lazy bodily stretching. Al-Samin says he may have begun stretching himself. Al-Tabrisi describes the bodily stretching as arising from listlessness."}]}
{"id": "75:33/q06", "question": "From what is يَتَمَطَّىٰ derived?", "turns_on": "The proposed root: back, stretching with consonant substitution, an ultimate dāl in madd, or maṭw.", "positions": [{"id": "75:33/q06/p1", "position": "From al-maṭā, the back, which the strutter twists or arches.", "reasons": "Al-Farra, al-Zajjaj, al-Tabari, Zayd ibn Aslam and many others connect the word to the back and its proud twisting or swaying. Bursevi specifies an alif substituted for wāw. Al-Majma', quoted by Tabataba'i, traces even lazy stretching back to arching the back. Al-Qurtubi mentions thick basin water called al-muṭīṭa because it spreads or stretches. Al-Tabrisi says the expression originally describes twisting one's back."}, {"id": "75:33/q06/p2", "position": "From yatamaṭṭaṭ or maṭṭ, stretching; a strutter extends his body or steps.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba compares
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

 the consonant change with yataẓannā from yataẓannan. Al-Tha'labi says an emphatic consonant becomes yāʾ; al-Nasafi and al-Samin say this avoids three like consonants, al-Samin adducing taẓannaytu, qaṣṣaytu aẓfārī and a verse with taqaḍḍī. Al-Razi compares taqaṣṣā from taqaṣṣaṣa. Al-Kashshaf, Ibn Ashur, Bursevi and Biqai explain the stretched stride; al-Samin says this root yields a sense close to the back derivation. Al-Qurtubi and al-Samin compare thick basin water whose name reflects spreading or extension. Al-Tabrisi also allows derivation from tamattuṭ, stretching, with a tāʾ changed to yāʾ, citing analogous forms."}, {"id": "75:33/q06/p3", "position": "Ultimately from madd, extending, with the root consonant originally dāl.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says maṭṭ and madd share a sense and pictures extending a hand while swaggering; Ibn al-Jawzi transmits this, and al-Jishumi also traces belly stretching to madd. Ibn al-Jawzi notes al-muṭayṭāʾ as the related gait."}, {"id": "75:33/q06/p4", "position": "From maṭw, stretching oneself.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi cites a report of Abu Bakr passing Bilal while Bilal stretched in the sun as usage for the sense."}]}
{"id": "75:33/q09", "question": "What physical conduct and judgment are attached to this gait?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "75:33/q09/p1", "position": "The strutter sways, extends or swings his arms, and the gait is censured.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari transmits a Prophetic criticism of al-muṭayṭāʾ as arm swinging and swaying. Al-Mawardi says the gait called al-maṭīṭā is prohibited. Al-Samin defines al-muṭayṭāʾ as strutting with extended arms; Bursevi says the hadith uses it for an extended gait and arms and explains al-ba's there as the severity of battle. Al-Tabrisi calls the exaggerated swaying walk al-muṭayṭāʾ and says it is prohibited."}]}
{"id": "75:38/q05", "question": "What do 'created and fashioned' describe in human development?", "turns_on": "How khalaqa and sawwā divide divine determination, embryonic shaping, spirit, functional fit, and possible maturation after birth.", "positions": [{"id": "75:38/q05/p1", "position": "God creates the embryo and proportionately forms it into a complete human being.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Wāḥidī, Bayḍāwī, and Ālūsī state the basic creation and completion; Ālūsī links the stages to 23:14. Naḥḥās specifies a speaking, hearing, seeing human; Thalabī includes the eventual male and female forms. Jishumī and Ṭabrisī specify internal and external organs in the womb; Jishumī also reports proportioning the clot into a human as people observe. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah describes a composite of elements becoming an independent person. Nasafī describes upright formation; Biqāʿī an adjusted independent new creation. Bursawī traces a further forty days to differentiable flesh, bones clothed with flesh, preparation for powers and spirit, and perfected proportion; he also reports the Mufradāt's explanation of perfection as formation conforming to divine wisdom. Iṣlāḥī describes provident shaping and perfection in the womb's darkness. Ibn ʿĀshūr defines taswiyah as straightening and making creation precise, with parallels in 91:7, 75:38, and 87:2; Asad directs readers to his notes on 87:2 and 91:7 for his rendering of sawwā, though the cited sentence breaks off."}, {"id": "75:38/q05/p2", "position": "God determines or measures the person's constitution, then forms and proportionately completes it.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports an interpretation that God creates, apportions, and proportions. Qurṭubī glosses khalaqa as determined and sawwā as fashioned and proportioned, including placement of the spirit. Biqāʿī specifies determination and formation of flesh, bones, nerves, other substances, and attributes. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says God measured and formed with adjustment and completion. Al-Zamakhsharī pairs creation with determination before perfect proportioning."}, {"id": "75:38/q05/p3", "position": "God breathes the spirit into the embryo, then completes its bodily formation.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil taking khalaqa as breathing the spirit and sawwā as completing the limbs. Baghawī also places the soul before proportional formation; Ibn al-Jawzī says God breathed the spirit and fashioned the creation."}, {"id": "75:38/q05/p4", "position": "God shapes the body and limbs, then breathes the spirit into it.", "reasons": "Bursawī reports Kāshifī's gloss of forming the person's shape and limbs and breathing the spirit. Ibn Kathīr says the clot becomes a morsel, is shaped and receives the spirit, becoming a sound, complete human by God's permission and decree."}, {"id": "75:38/q05/p5", "position": "God creates the human in the womb, then brings bodily strength and movement to maturity after birth.", "reasons": "Māwardī gives this as one possibility; Ṭabrisī reports a similar view, saying the person is made human after birth and strength is completed."}, {"id": "75:38/q05/p6", "position": "God creates bodies and fits each limb for its particular action.", "reasons": "Māwardī and Ṭabrisī both give this explanation, assigning each limb its own function."}, {"id": "75:38/q05/p7", "position": "Fashioning matches each paired bodily organ with its counterpart.", "reasons": "Bursawī reports this as another explanation of proportioning."}]}
{"id": "76:25/q01", "question": "What practice does remembering the Lord's name call for?", "turns_on": "Whether the imperative denotes prescribed prayer, comprehensive devotion, praise by heart and tongue, affirmation of oneness within prayer, or an inward realization.", "positions": [{"id": "76:25/q01/p1", "position": "It includes sustained remembrance in worship, supplication, proclamation, and other devotion, including prescribed and voluntary prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it persistent remembrance, with night prostration, prayer or saying subḥān Allāh. Bayḍāwī and Bursawī allow remembrance alongside the prayer reading; Bursawī says morning to evening means all times. Ibn ʿĀshūr includes preaching, obligatory and voluntary worship, exhortation through fear and hope, supplication and seeking forgiveness; 11:114–115 calls prayer remembrance. Elmalılı includes invocation, the call to prayer and prayer, citing 2:153. Kur'an Yolu prefers broad worship and devotion, especially night prayer with glorification, supplication, repentance and forgiveness. Study Quran's Aj also allows remembrance every moment."}, {"id": "76:25/q01/p2", "position": "It is prayer or naming God in the daily prayers.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī has calling on God during dawn, noon and afternoon prayer. Baghawī takes night prostrations as Maghrib and Isha and long night glorification as voluntary prayer after the obligatory prayers. Biqāʿī calls prayer the best bodily worship because tongue, heart and limbs jointly affirm God's existence and oneness. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 11:114–115 for prayer as remembrance. Study Quran reports Aj, JJ and Ṭs for naming God in daily prayers. The Kashshāf author reads the command as maintaining the dawn and afternoon prayers."}, {"id": "76:25/q01/p3", "position": "It is verbal and inward praise of God throughout the day and night.", "reasons": "Rāzī says remembrance by heart and tongue at all times, citing 33:41–42. Kur'an Yolu reports Rāzī's second reading as verbal glorification and belief in God's transcendence throughout day and night."}, {"id": "76:25/q01/p4", "position": "It is affirming God's oneness in prayer.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies three takbīrs and testimony to God's oneness at each of Fajr and Maghrib, repudiating shirk. Wāḥidī and Ibn al-Jawzī likewise explain remembrance as affirming oneness in prayer."}, {"id": "76:25/q01/p5", "position": "It is realizing one's Essence as God's greatest Name and manifesting its rights and perfections.", "reasons": "Qāshānī places this from primordial beginning to end. Bursawī reports Qāshānī's formulation from the rise of divine light to its setting and concealment."}]}
{"id": "76:25/q06", "question": "Which prayers are assigned to morning and evening remembrance?", "turns_on": "The span of aṣīl and whether the time references denote a subset of prescribed prayers or the five prayers together with the next verse.", "positions": [{"id": "76:25/q06/p1", "position": "Fajr, Zuhr and Asr; in a five prayer reading, Maghrib and Isha follow in the night command.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Māwardī, Wāḥidī reporting ʿAṭāʾ, al-Kalbī and Muqātil, Qurṭubī, Nasafī, Bayḍāwī, Biqāʿī, Bursawī and Elmalılı assign the three daytime prayers. Ibn al-Jawzī gives noon and afternoon together as an alternative to Asr alone. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports Ibn Ḥabīb and others mapping the surrounding times to all five prayers; Rāzī reports a group doing likewise, with long night glorification as night vigil. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Zayd on five prescribed prayers, with evening including noon and glorification denoting night prayer. Kur'an Yolu reports Rāzī's five prayer account and says extended night worship is obligatory for the Prophet but recommended for his community. Baghawī says night prostrations are Maghrib and Isha, followed by voluntary worship. Biqāʿī says other prayers occur in the following phrase."}, {"id": "76:25/q06/p2", "position": "Fajr and Asr.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī gives Asr as one reading of aṣīl. Biqāʿī says dawn and afternoon prayers were the only early Islamic prescriptions and were two cycles each. The Kashshāf author assigns morning and evening remembrance to maintaining the dawn and afternoon prayers."}, {"id": "76:25/q06/p3", "position": "Fajr and Zuhr.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī reports Ibn Zayd assigning al-aṣīl to Zuhr. Ālūsī allows Fajr and Zuhr, explaining that aṣīl can cover noon to sunset."}, {"id": "76:25/q06/p4", "position": "Fajr and Maghrib.", "reasons": "Muqātil says each has three takbīrs and testimony to God's oneness, repudiating shirk."}, {"id": "76:25/q06/p5", "position": "The two evening prayers.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī us
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

es this designation for morning and evening remembrance; he separately assigns night prostration and long glorification to voluntary night prayer."}]}
{"id": "76:26/q01", "question": "What does 'from the night' specify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:26/q01/p1", "position": "A portion of the night is set aside for worship and prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Biqai says the remainder is for sleep and rest. Al-Baydawi and Alusi specify prayer; Elmalili explicitly glosses min as partitive. Al-Nahhas supplies an understood 'from the night' with the command. The Kashshaf's author illustrates partitive min by comparing 71:4, 'He forgives you some of your sins.'"}]}
{"id": "76:26/q02", "question": "What does prostrating to Him at night mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the prostration command identifies the two prescribed evening prayers or night prayer more generally.", "positions": [{"id": "76:26/q02/p1", "position": "It refers specifically to the Maghrib and Isha prayers.", "reasons": "Al-Biqai calls prostration the prayer's most excellent act; Alusi and Elmalili take the part to name the whole prayer. Al-Suyuti's Itqan illustrates this figure with prayer's standing, recitation, bowing, and prostration standing for prayer, alongside examples involving face and hands (55:27, 2:144, 88:8, 88:3, 2:286, 2:184, 17:78, 2:43, 5:95). Al-Baydawi and Bursevi phrase the identification tentatively. Muqatil names Isha before sleep, and al-Mawardi calls them sunset and late-night prayers."}, {"id": "76:26/q02/p2", "position": "It directs prayer at night generally, whether obligatory or voluntary.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur locates this prayer when the Prophet is free from public preaching and cites 73:2, 73:20. Al-Tabari explains it as praying and glorifying at night; Ibn Abbas likewise says prayer and glorification. Elmalili says prostration explains remembrance as prayer by naming a part for the whole. Ibn Kathir compares the night-vigil commands in 17:79 and 73:1-4. The Kashshaf's author gives prayer during part of the night as an alternative to identifying the two evening prayers."}]}
{"id": "79:18/q01", "question": "What does “هل لك” convey in Moses’ address?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:18/q01/p1", "position": "It asks whether Pharaoh has a desire, need, or inclination toward the offered purification, in an established idiom of invitation.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī and al-Bursevī gloss the desire or need; al-Elmalılı adds intention. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a concise fixed invitation, like asking a guest to stay, and cites Kaʿb’s هل لك فيما and Bujayr’s هل لك في التي. Al-Rāzī compares هل لك في. Al-Samīn gives هل لك في الخير as an idiom for رغبة. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī takes the question as asking inclination. Ibn Kathīr frames the invitation as accepting a way that purifies Pharaoh."}]}
{"id": "79:18/q04", "question": "What purification does “تزكى” invite Pharaoh to seek?", "turns_on": "Whether purification is the initial move to faith, its declaration, good conduct, comprehensive moral growth, repentance from tyranny, inward self-effacement, or charity; the charity gloss is disputed in Pharaoh's unbelieving context.", "positions": [{"id": "79:18/q04/p1", "position": "To leave unbelief or shirk and embrace faith, Islam, and God's oneness.", "reasons": "Muqātil includes repairing corruption and accepting God's oneness. Al-Ṭabarī says pure belief; Ibn Zayd links this sense throughout the Qur'an to Islam, citing 20:76 and 80:3, 7. Al-Fārisī and al-Wāḥidī cite 91:9 and 18:74 for purification from shirk, al-Fārisī also 80:7. Al-Māwardī transmits Qatāda. Al-Baghawī says both readings indicate escape from shirk, Islam, and uprightness. Al-Rāzī says the invitation includes monotheism and religious law. Others mention rebellion, tyranny, obedience, or freeing Israel as extensions of the change. Ibn Kathīr glosses the requested purification as submitting and obeying."}, {"id": "79:18/q04/p2", "position": "To cleanse deficiencies and vices and acquire virtues: a full moral purification that includes faith.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says restricting the sense to conversion or the declaration is too narrow. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Biqāʿī agree; al-Biqāʿī specifies outward and inward vices, with faith and freeing Israel as the lowest beginning. Al-Bursevī adds the opacity of human and natural conditions. Al-Elmalılı adds growth in Islamic qualities; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ adds growth of the soul's virtues. Al-Rāzī speaks of every defect and what is unfitting."}, {"id": "79:18/q04/p3", "position": "To profess that there is no deity but God.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī reports ʿIkrima. Al-Wāḥidī reports Ibn ʿAbbās, and also Muqātil's related formulation of affirming divine oneness. Al-Baghawī reports Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Qurṭubī transmits it through al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Qushayrī reports a promise attached to the declaration: an imperishable kingdom, ageless youth, four hundred years of comfort, then paradise. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the formula is contained in a broader purification."}, {"id": "79:18/q04/p4", "position": "To do good.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Wāḥidī both report this gloss from al-Kalbī."}, {"id": "79:18/q04/p5", "position": "To repent of tyranny and return to God.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this reading, with ensuing faith-driven fear motivating obedience and restraining sin."}, {"id": "79:18/q04/p6", "position": "In an inward reading, to annihilate selfhood.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says guidance to fear is knowledge of the unity of the Essence, which softens and dissolves selfhood."}, {"id": "79:18/q04/p7", "position": "To give alms.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAmr's explanation derives this from assimilated تتزكى. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Khālawayh reject applying it here because Moses first called an unbeliever to belief, not charity; Ibn Khālawayh cites the wording زكية in 18:74. Al-Qurṭubī reports Abū ʿAmr's preference for the light reading and belief sense."}]}

{"id": "79:19/q04", "question": "What does 'then you will fear' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the fear is explained by religious conduct and punishment or by Qashani's inward account of divine unity and loss of selfhood.", "positions": [{"id": "79:19/q04/p1", "position": "Pharaoh would fear God and His punishment, with reverence expressed in duties and avoidance of disobedience.", "reasons": "Jishumi equates khashya with khawf, fear. {"id": "79:23/q04", "question": "In what order did the gathering and call occur?", "turns_on": "Whether the two verbs give the event's actual chronology or a sequence whose real order Ibn ʿAbbās reverses.", "positions": [{"id": "79:23/q04/p1", "position": "He gathered the people and then called out to them.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī reports Ibn Zayd's sequence: the crowd assembled, Pharaoh declared himself their highest lord, then God punished him in both lives (79:24–25). {"id": "79:24/q07", "question": "What lordship did Pharaoh claim by 'your highest lord'?", "turns_on": "What Pharaoh counted as a 'lord': supreme deity, other gods or idols, human authorities, benefactor, proximate deity, inherited divine status, or apportioned divine nature.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q07/p1", "position": "He claimed supreme lordship, with no lord above him.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, Bursawī and Elmalılı give the no-higher-lord sense. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the wording and 28:38 and 26:29 support actual divinity rather than mere kingship."}, {"id": "79:24/q07/p2", "position": "He ranked himself above the gods or idols his people acknowledged.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ says he made little idols for the people, told them to worship them, and claimed lordship of idols and worshipers; al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī transmit this interpretation. Ibn ʿĀshūr offers the idea that Pharaoh was regarded as lord of many gods, making 'highest' explanatory. Al-Burhān reconciles 7:127 by saying the gods were his property and he first worshiped them in the people's religion before demanding the top rank. Al-Thaʿlabī reports an unnamed explanation that calls the idols lords and makes Pharaoh lord of both the idols and the people."}, {"id": "79:24/q07/p3", "position": "He claimed supremacy over other human lords, leaders, kings, and officials.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī report a hierarchy of chiefs over lower people; al-Bayḍāwī speaks of everyone managing people's affairs, and Bursawī of kings and officials. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports a political reading like Pharaoh's boast of Egypt's kingdom in 43:51, but rejects it as conflicting with the apparent wording and 28:38 and 26:29."}, {"id": "79:24/q07/p4", "position": "He meant that he alone nurtured, benefited, commanded and forbade his people, while denying a Creator and resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and Bursawī portray Pharaoh as a materialist. For al-Rāzī, ربكم refers to nurturer and benefactor, since Pharaoh denied a deity and messenger. Both deny that he claimed to have created the cosmos: that would be self-evidently false, and a person insane enough to doubt a Creator could not have been sent a prophet."}, {"id": "79:24/q07/p5", "position": "He claimed to be the deity closest to people, administering their provisions, affairs and honor, unlike other gods.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī offers this possible meaning and cites 7:127."}, {"id": "79:24/q07/p6", "position": "He claimed the status of Amun-Ra's son and successor.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr offers this alternative, explaining that Egyptian priests called the king Amun-Ra's son and held the sun to be that god's manifestation."}, {"id": "79:24/q07/p7", "position": "He assumed divinity was a nature distributed among beings and that its highest possessor could best obtain what he wanted.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī identifies this as Pharaoh's premise behind ranking lords."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q11", "question": "How did this claim follow Pharaoh's earlier claim in 28:38?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q11/p1", "position": "He first said he knew no god for his people besides himself, then later claimed to be their highest lord.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid link both claims to God's seizure of Pharaoh. {"id": "79:24/q19", "question": "What does Pharaoh's boast show about divine power and the gravity of his sin?", "turns_on": "Whether the note stresses culpability and punishment or specifically refutes an asserted divine power.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q19/p1", "position": "It is a grave claim to divinity for which Pharaoh was seized and punished.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid say God seized him for both divinity claims. {"id": "79:25/q03", "question": "What does نَكَالَ mean?", "turns_on": "The sense emphasized: exemplary deterrence, fettered humiliation, or incapacity.", "positions": [{"id": "79:25/q03/p1", "position": "A severe exemplary punishment that deters others.", "reasons": "Jishumi derives it from prevention, comparing shackles and refraining.
